newsitem.title: USA: INSIGHT-June T-bonds await departure from 110 area.
newsitem.headline: INSIGHT-June T-bonds await departure from 110 area.

text.p: The 110 area is becoming an increasingly pivotal level for June U.S. Treasury bond futures after a reversal rally from early lows today again yanked the market back there, technical analysts said.
The contract has been seesawing within one point of 110-00 ever since the start of the month, except for a brief dip to 108-30/32 on May 8.
"A break from this area is going to be very important," said Stewart Taylor, president of Taylor Consulting.
June bonds today fell to a low of 109-12/32 early and then bounced above 110-00 in trading driven by economic indicators.

Some analysts have cited the 100-day and 200-day moving averages drifting near 110, while others saw as the magnet the high level of open interest in the 110 strike price in June T-bond futures options, which expire on Friday.

Opinion was divided on whether the range trade after a sharp rally from April lows was a basing pattern for more advances or a signal for a major reversal, but most analysts expected a down move fairly soon, either from the current level or from somewhere slightly higher.
Taylor said surprises here would be to the downside, given the rise in futures open interest on the market's way up.

"I think the market is much more vulnerable to long liquidation than it is to short-covering," Taylor said. "I think it's been a corrective rally and it's either over or is very, very close to being over."

David Ging, Treasury market strategist at Donaldson, Lufkin & Jenrette, expected the market to grind a little higher going into next Tuesday's Federal Open Market Committee meeting before losing steam.
He said momentum indicators were generally positive, although some were starting to show weakness, with signs of bearish divergence in the shorter-term ones.
Bearish divergence occurs when oscillator indicators make lower highs or lower lows as the market fluctuates.

He said Tuesday's 110-22/32 high was obvious resistance but more important levels where bonds could stall were 110-30/32, the 61.8 percent retracement of the February-April decline, and the 111-6/32 area, where a down channel line from December highs came in.

Taylor said the surrounding environment also did not bode well for bonds, particularly the dollar's slide against the yen and a rise in the Commodity Research Bureau index, which has broken above its August 1996 highs near 252.

"A daily close above 252 is very, very bad news," he said. "You have to say you've broken out. That's the last real resistance until you get all the way back up to the 264 high that was set in early 1996."
Numerous studies have shown that the CRB index does not have very high correlation with inflation rates, he said, but it does have a strong negative correlation with bond prices.
"We're not so concerned with inflation as we are with bond prices," he said.
